title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
titleZh: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
author: linolevan
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.
New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’
The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.

It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server.

comments.author: pen2l
comments.textRawHtml:
Apple, to me, is the winner in the end of this AI chapter.

Distillation works: we can get models leaner, have better performance with lesser and lesser parameters, more efficient, running locally. Apple gets this and we'll see the result with M7 Max/ultra chips and I reckon this will be one of the titular apps when M7 line of chips are introduced.

I guess it explains the haste Anthropic and OpenAI are in to IPO, cash out and leave the the retail investor holding the bag.

children.author: aurareturn
children.textRawHtml:
Apple, to me, is the winner in the end of this AI chapter.
I might be one of only few people who think Apple is a loser in the AI chapter.

I don't think it shows yet but I think the dominance of the App Store will end. I think a ton of iOS apps will be replaced by ChatGPT/Claude. I think there is a big opening for a company to redesign the phone from the ground up purely around an AI assistant instead of apps.

I think AI will severely weaken iOS, App Store, and the iPhone in the next few years. It was nearly impossible to start a 3rd competitor to iOS and Android until recently because no one is going to redesign their apps for your new phone. Today, that's different. Many productivity apps are just being replaced by GenAI/ChatGPT/etc and services are making it easy for AI agents to access directly without an app.

Not to mention higher chip prices will eat into hardware margins.

I do not think local LLM inference will make up for lesser iPhone dominance.

children.author: smugglerFlynn
children.textRawHtml:
Replacing a good app is still extremely hard. Let me explain.

Commodities like todo apps and calculators rarely compete on features, they compete on product design. This includes look and feel, relation between elements, design choices on what exact common features are available.

All products are, at their essence, just a set of design decisions stitched and shipped together.

Now, making these design decisions is hard. It requires knowledge, consistency, and insights into how real people operate real products. Even as a sole user of the app you build you rarely know what you actually need.

LLMs are 'design-less' in their essence. Building your own todo app takes literal seconds and it all looks simple because LLMs will default most of these design decisions for you - until you try to use your new app daily and notice it somehow sucks. Building a good todo app or good calculator requires tweaking, publishing, polishing, and solving bugs, testing, rinse and repeat.

Another tricky side of this is that you might know logically what features you want, but you are not selecting one product over another logically. You need to try and see if that works for you, all the vibes and good parts and bad parts and design choices and colors, till you find something that "clicks" for you. Using pure Claude as a todo app only works as long as you want to have more Claude in your daily life.

In the meantime app store provides dozens of well-reviewed alternative solutions which look good and require zero maintenance.

And that's just a calculator or todo app. Non-commodity apps are even harder than that.

children.author: WarmWash
children.textRawHtml:
Design is dead (long live design)

I don't see any future where programs follow the static nature of old paradigm programming. A nice intuitive UI? What about just telling the app what I need when I need it? The gold standard of consumer UI is...another person.

If I have a team of god tier light speed SWE's at my disposal, why the fuck am I fumbling around in an actions panel? The program can just be dynamically modified in near real time to be whatever I need it to be in that moment.

If you extrapolate LLMs out to their extreme, you get a shape-shifting liquid array of bits in memory that manifest anything at the behest of a completely natural language interface.

children.author: spider-mario
children.textRawHtml:
> The gold standard of consumer UI is...another person.

Absolutely not. Constraining the set of possible actions instead of having you verbalise what you want every time is often a feature, not just a technical limitation. A camera with a shutter button is better design than having to tell the camera “please take a photo”.

At the supermarket, I personally also prefer the self-checkout machines over going to a human cashier.

children.author: WarmWash
children.textRawHtml:
It wouldn't be just verbalizing, you could type or gesture just as well. Nor would you need to communicate each command, the machine would recognize that you want a button for your camera, the checkout would understand that you want to checkout and understand each intended action as you do so.

The UI is totally fluid at all times, because an "intelligence" is actively manifesting it at all times. Nothing needs to be hard coded.

children.author: p_j_w
children.textRawHtml:
No it absolutely is not. I spent a good 2 weekends using an agent to develop an alternative to a website that I didn't care to pay for. After all of that time, while it's functional and I do occasionally use it for its intended purpose, if you take into account the amount I paid in tokens and the amount of time I spent on it, the average Joe would've been better off just paying for the site, which is actually still better.

The only reason it works out in my favor is that I enjoyed doing it. Normal people don't want to fuck around with that kind of shit.

children.author: WarmWash
children.textRawHtml:
If your stance is that AI will never be able to eclipse human design, then yes it's an impossible hurdle t overcome.

But already AI design is everywhere and regular people don't even notice (outside perhaps the intentional cues in mainstream image generators). It's only going to get better as people can interact with the design the same as the interact with another person.

children.author: oinj
children.textRawHtml:
You are assuming that you'll always have the time and energy to determine what you need at the moment you need it, which doesn't really sound true.

You're also assuming that there are no negatives to saying what you want compared to just acting on things, but since the beginning of computing many people have proven this wrong time and again. I suggest you read about HCI as a research field and its history, it doesn't take much to realise how limited the average HNer's understanding of UI/UX design is, and how far current LLMs are from the skills required to be able to carefully design an app for productive human use.

children.author: gls2ro
children.textRawHtml:
Unless AI will be ar the level of saying "I want a scheduling app that fits me" I still see value in buying some apps.

I like to customize my Neovim setup or terminal and a bunch of scripts that I keep making them nice and maybe my blog and so on.

I don't want to become the PM of every app I need. But I do agree changes will happen to the current apps and how we buy and use them. Not sure exactly where it will settle. But still unknown unknowns and domain knowledge and vocabulary is not yet allowing anyone to build their own apps unless for simple cases.

Or maybe it is just me: I want someone else to think about my accounting app. I dont want to spend time to learn and understand and keep myself up to date or setup a series of LLM sessions that navigate and watch laws and propose changes.

children.author: WarmWash
children.textRawHtml:
Why do you need a scheduling app when you have a secretary?

Why do you need an accounting app when you have an accountant?

Programs of the future will in no way resemble what they are today. I don't even want to call it a "program" because in my head it's more like an intelligent digital liquid that can rapidly flow into any state. This flash-in-the-pan 50 year archaic era of software will look like what the oil lamp looks like today. A crude intermediate tech during a time of much larger transition.

children.author: sterlind
children.textRawHtml:
it's nice to see what's on my schedule at a glance, rather than needing to ask my secretary. also helps with situational awareness.

it's nice to see my financial situation at a glance, without asking my accountant.

speech/text is one modality. we humans are also visual and tactile. and we need consistency and recurring patterns of interaction to function well.
